chapter_theme: In the Mokkala debate Neelakesi and the Buddhist thera argue over whether a quality and its substance are one or different, how atoms join into matter, and the Jain claim that a thing exists and does not exist in different respects; he attacks it with the gooseberry, the elephant, the bull's horn, the hare's horn and right and left hands, and she answers by separating substance from state, real things from fictions, and naming from existence.

cast.role: the demoness converted to the Jain dharma, now its debater
the Buddhist thera (தேரன்) whom Neelakesi debates in the Mokkala sarukkam

391.reading: Answering the cooked-pulse example, Neelakesi says the gross pulse changes in its way and the water too passes off as vapour, so that when both are spent together into the mash it is folly to grant a change to one and deny it to the other.
391.nuance: The verse replies to 390, where the Buddhist mocks pulse and water boiled together into கும்மாயம்; the example is the stock Jain one for a substance that persists through change. Line 1 (பாவியுண்டா) is hard to construe, and the speaker is inferred from the alternation of என்றான் and என்றாள்.

claims.claim: when pulse and water are cooked into one dish both undergo change, so neither alone can be said to persist unchanged

392.reading: The Buddhist objects that if perishing, arising and persisting are qualities, then the thing that perishes, arises and persists would have to be some further substance, and asks what that could be.
392.nuance: He takes the Jain triad of origination, persistence and destruction and tries to force it into a split between qualities and a bearer that is never found, which suits his own view that there is no lasting substance behind momentary events.

claims.claim: if arising, persisting and perishing are qualities, the substance that bears them must be something else that cannot be named

393.reading: Neelakesi replies that the quality spoken of is the qualified substance itself and the substance is never apart from its many qualities, so she holds them both different and one, and his confusion is to treat these as contradictory.
393.nuance: This is the Jain position of difference-in-identity (வேறென ஒன்றென) between quality and substance, stated against the Buddhist demand for one or the other; the Jain refuses the either-or rather than choosing a side.

claims.claim: quality and qualified substance are both different and one, and holding both is no contradiction

394.reading: The Buddhist asks the woman who holds the scripture how matter (புற்கலம்), the primary substance, joining with itself, spreads out as stones, water, earth and fire, and whether the things that meet enter into one another.
394.nuance: புற்கலம் here is the Jain pudgala, matter, not the Buddhist Pudgalavada person of 248. தியம் in line 3 is not a word I can construe; the sense of the question is clear from 395 to 397.

claims.claim: atoms that combine into gross things must either interpenetrate or stay apart, and either way the Jain account fails

395.reading: Neelakesi tells him to hear what the scripture lays down: the atoms have qualities fit for binding, are hard to separate once joined, and, setting aside the classes that do not bind, build up from the two-atom compound onward.
395.nuance: The appeal is to ஓத்து, the Jain canon; the rule of excluded classes (நீத்த வருக்க நெறிமை) seems to be the doctrine that only atoms of certain degrees of quality bind, but the line is compressed.

claims.claim: atoms bind by qualities of their own and build compounds upward from the two-atom unit

396.reading: The thera argues that if the aggregate (கந்தம்) rises from the dyad upward, then atoms that crowd together and touch must, being round, have an inside and sides, and so are seen to be divisible.
396.nuance: கந்தம் here is the aggregate of atoms, not the Buddhist five aggregates; the argument, that contact implies parts and parts deny indivisibility, is the Buddhist objection to atoms in general.

claims.claim: an atom that touches another must have an inside and sides, and so cannot be indivisible

397.reading: Neelakesi says he prattles in giving an inside and sides to a primary substance that holds one place, enlarging it to split it, and answers that by sharing the same place atoms reach plurality and become form, as happens even with cognition.
397.nuance: The reply seems to rest on the Jain view that many atoms can occupy one point of space, so that combination does not require parts; the comparison with அறிவு in line 3 is obscure.

claims.claim: atoms that occupy one and the same place can become many and take form without being divided

398.reading: The Buddhist, whom the narrator calls great in the dharma that gives away women, mocks her: the hill gooseberry is in her hand, and at that very moment she will say it is not in Uraiyur, as if this were a truth hard for others to see.
398.nuance: He parodies the Jain claim that a thing exists from its own place and does not exist from another as a truism. The narrator's epithet (பெண்டானம் ஈயும் அறம்) turns Neelakesi's earlier charge about the bodhisattva who gave his wives into a sneer at the speaker.

claims.claim: that a fruit held here does not exist in a distant town is a truism, not a hidden truth

399.reading: He goes on that everyone knows fire is hot, water cold and wind thin, and says that if she says these are Buddha's words she will not call them false, yet she has spoiled them like a whole pot of gruel.
399.nuance: The run of lines 3 and 4 is unclear: who calls what false and what the gruel (முழுக்கூழ்) stands for cannot be fixed from the verse alone.

claims.claim: the plain natures everyone perceives, such as the heat of fire and the cold of water, need no qualification

400.reading: He adds that she would call the rutting elephant tied to the post non-existent, though when it has come and stands here its existence cannot be denied, and curses her words; the narrator names him as one who has seen a release like a burnt seed.
400.nuance: The closing epithet (வெந்து ... வித்தின் அனைத்தாகிய வீடு) gives the Buddhist release as a seed burnt so it cannot sprout again; whether the narrator means it as praise or as the Jain view of nirvana as extinction is not said.

claims.claim: what is plainly present before one cannot be called non-existent

401.reading: Neelakesi answers that she called the thing non-existent there and existent where it is, stating non-existence and existence together, and that he finishes only the arguments he wants and will not also say the same of her Lord whom the gods throng to worship in the golden fort.
401.nuance: This answers 398 to 400: the Jain claim is not that the gooseberry or the elephant is absent, but that existence and non-existence each hold in their own respect. The point of line 4 about the Lord in the golden fort is unclear.

claims.claim: a thing is non-existent from another place and existent where it is, and both are said together

402.reading: The Buddhist says that if the horn of the killing bull is non-existent in the young calf, then, since she speaks of existence and non-existence together, she should say the calf is the killing bull at that very time.

claims.claim: if existence and non-existence hold of one thing at once, the calf must already be the bull

403.reading: Neelakesi replies that a difference of thing is spoken of only when the bull has arisen; for the calf not yet grown, non-existence comes first while the existence of the substance stands firm, and nowhere does either change.
403.nuance: She separates the persisting substance from its states: the horn is a state not yet arisen, so its absence in the calf is prior non-existence and not the absence of the animal. கலைக்கு in line 4 is unclear.

claims.claim: the horn's absence in the calf is the prior non-existence of a state, while the substance persists throughout

404.reading: He counters that a calf, a hare, the beast called donkey and a hill never come to have a horn on the head as a limb, so her distinction fails, and some things are simply non-existent in some respects.
404.nuance: The hare's and donkey's horns are the stock examples of what never exists; why கன்று (calf) appears in this list, after the calf of 402 that does grow horns, is unclear.

claims.claim: some things, like the horn of a hare or donkey, never arise, so their non-existence is not a matter of standpoint

405.reading: Neelakesi says no one speaks of distinctions by taking up a horn that does not exist as if it did; if he wants distinctions he must learn the existence and non-existence of things that cannot stand without joining, or else he too is granting the donkey a horn.
405.nuance: Her reply limits the scope of her own doctrine: existence and non-existence in respects are said of real substances and their states, not of fictions.

claims.claim: existence and non-existence in respects are said only of real things, not of fictions like a hare's horn

406.reading: Mokkalan laughs: there is no right or left hand except by relation, she says the same of that, she of great cunning has quickly understood both to exist, and she is very good indeed.
406.nuance: The praise is sarcasm; his point is that relational terms like right and left have no being of their own.

claims.claim: right and left exist only by relation and have no being of their own

407.reading: Neelakesi answers that if a thing exists only by this relation, both sides arise together, so each side becomes void and the limbs too, and tells him to go round now like the shaft of an oil press, which is his safety.
407.nuance: The oil-press image mocks an argument that goes in circles; the middle of the verse is compressed.

claims.claim: if relation alone gave things their being, both relata and everything else would become empty

408.reading: He replies that hands and feet do not get their being from relation, since the body must have the parts named, and says she has made the little humans of the world into lumps of clay.
408.nuance: குழமண்ணர்களா in line 3 is obscure and the turn of his argument is hard to follow; he seems to concede that limbs are not merely relational.

409.reading: Neelakesi says the hands, which exist by relation to the feet, also come to be by their own former nature, and that if he asks in what way they exist, his conclusion makes him like the dog and the crab.
409.nuance: The dog and crab comparison is an insult whose point is lost; the doctrine seems to be that a thing has both its own nature and a relational one.

claims.claim: a limb has both its own prior nature and a nature from relation

410.reading: The Buddhist says she demands that the word 'is not' (அல்) in his scripture mean 'does not exist' (இல்), and asks whether one who says 'that is not a dog, it is a jackal' is saying the jackal does not exist.
410.nuance: He separates negation of identity (அல்) from negation of existence (இல்), a distinction Tamil grammar itself draws.

claims.claim: saying a thing is not this is not saying it does not exist

411.reading: Neelakesi says that when the cognition 'dog or jackal?' arises he claimed that 'not' is known only after examining both words, that he does not know words or seek the way of those who know, and that prattling many words is what ghosts do.
411.nuance: Line 2 seems to report his position before she dismisses it; her answer is mostly scorn, not a counter-argument.

412.reading: The thera, smiling a little at the woman with the chosen garland, says she claims a thing that does not exist has neither name nor cognition, and asks whether dependence, separation, meeting and the absence of a mind are not named so only for want of knowing.
412.nuance: சார்வு is the Buddhist term for dependent arising; the list in line 2 seems meant as names for absences or relations that have no substance, but the force of line 3 (உணராமையிற்கு) is uncertain.
412.event: The Buddhist thera smiles at Neelakesi.

claims.claim: names and cognitions do occur for what does not exist

413.reading: Neelakesi asks whether anyone, even a common man, who studied the meaning the Trustworthy One gave in that scripture could fail to know, and says that of all he has dragged in he cannot name one by the scripture's account that has a name and a cognition but no existence.
413.nuance: ஆத்தன் is the Apta, the trustworthy teacher, the Jain title for the Jina; சாத்தன் stands for anyone at all. The appeal is to scripture, but made as a debating challenge.

claims.claim: one who studies the meaning the Trustworthy One gave in the scripture cannot fail to know
nothing that has a name and a cognition is wholly non-existent

414.reading: The Buddhist says she always holds that the nature of one thing does not belong to another, yet water heated as iron is heated stirs and takes on fire's quality, and if so her long thesis is diminished.
414.nuance: He turns a Jain thesis against itself with heated water. The reply is not in this chapter: 415 turns to the soul in the body, which may be her answer by analogy, but the text does not say so.

claims.claim: the quality of one thing passes into another, as heated water takes on fire's heat

links.note: The Jain in Manimekalai 27 gives gram cooked into கும்மாயம் as his example of a kind that persists while a form passes; in Neelakesi 390 to 391 the Buddhist attacks that very example and Neelakesi defends it.
links.teaches: The cooked-gram example is shown to be a fixed Jain teaching case known to both sides, so the Buddhist epic's report of Jain doctrine matches what the Jain epic itself has to defend.

links.note: Manimekalai's Jain states that every thing takes on origination, persistence and destruction in each instant; Neelakesi 392 has the Buddhist ask what bears those three if they are qualities.
links.teaches: Manimekalai lets the Jain triad stand unanswered, while the Jain epic shows the Buddhist's actual objection to it, the missing bearer, and the Jain reply in 393 that quality and bearer are one and different.

links.note: The Vaisheshika in Manimekalai 27 lists substance and quality as separate categories, substance bearing quality; Neelakesi says the quality is the qualified substance itself and the two are both different and one.
links.teaches: Against the Vaisheshika separation of substance and quality, the Jain refuses both their separateness and their simple identity, so the two schools disagree on whether a quality can be counted apart from its bearer.

links.note: Manimekalai's Jain says only that the atom, matter (புற்கலம்), is the outward form of things; Neelakesi 395 to 397 defends how atoms become form against the objection that touching atoms must have parts.
links.teaches: The bare formula in the Buddhist epic hides a live problem, how indivisible atoms can join, which the Jain epic answers with many atoms sharing one place.

links.note: Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher gives the hare's horn as the case of what has no arising at all; Neelakesi's Buddhist uses the hare's and donkey's horns to show that some things are non-existent outright.
links.teaches: The Jain epic's Buddhist argues with the same stock example the Buddhist epic teaches, so here the polemic reproduces Buddhist doctrine fairly before Neelakesi answers it in 405.

links.note: Manimekalai's teacher lists modes of usage that rest on what is not (இல்லது சார்ந்த வழக்கு), and pairs cognition with the hare's horn; Neelakesi's Buddhist insists that names and cognitions occur for what does not exist.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows the Buddhist claim in 412 rests on a worked-out doctrine of usage, which is what Neelakesi's reply in 413 must deny by appeal to scripture.

links.note: In 243 Neelakesi charges that the bodhisattva gave away his wives and took that as dharma; in 398 the narrator names the Buddhist debater as great in the dharma that gives away women.
links.teaches: A charge made once in argument has become the narrator's standing epithet for the Buddhist side, so the poem's narration takes Neelakesi's part even in describing the speaker.

links.note: 392 asks what bears arising, persisting and perishing; 403 applies the answer to the calf and the bull, whose horn arises while the substance persists.
links.teaches: The abstract triad of 392 to 393 is turned into a test case in 403, which shows what the Jain means by persistence: the animal's substance, not its horn.

links.note: Tirumular says the wise gave up disputation (தர்க்க வாதம்) and gained release by reciting the Veda; Neelakesi appeals to the Apta's scripture as what leaves nothing unknown, but does so as a move in a debate.
links.teaches: Both rest final authority on a scripture, but the Saiva verse sets scripture against argument while the Jain debater uses scripture as the ground of argument, so the two disagree about whether debate serves the scripture.

gains.a: the Jain appeal to scripture is seen as one way to end a dispute, which a rival tradition takes as reason to give up disputing
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of argument is seen as a choice, since another scriptural tradition put argument at the centre of its practice

links.note: Naladiyar 313 describes people who rush to debate on the strength of a word, talk at length and do not know when they are beaten; Neelakesi tells the Buddhist he does not know words and prattles many words like a ghost.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's type of the endless talker becomes a charge thrown by one debater at another, which shows the description used as a weapon in debate as well as a moral portrait.

gains.a: Neelakesi's insult is placed within a known ethical type, the speaker who does not know when he is beaten
gains.b: the quatrain gains a scene where its charge is made by a party to the dispute, which shows that calling the other side a prattler is itself a debating move

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id differs from vaadham, which the list already uses for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: a quality, as against the substance (குணி) that bears it; whether the two are one or different is argued between schools
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' words: குணம் (392, 393, 395), குணி and குணிப்பொருள் (393), தீக்குணம் (414)

new_concepts.gloss: dependent arising: the twelve linked conditions from ignorance to the fruit of deeds through which birth arises
new_concepts.label_source: the Manimekalai's term; here the Buddhist's word சார்வு (412 line 2)

source_issues: 391 line 1 (பாவியுண்டா) and 394 line 3 (தியம்) cannot be construed with confidence.
397 line 3 (ஆரிடமாய) and 403 line 4 (கலைக்குண்மை) are obscure; 408 line 3 (குழமண்ணர்களா) is not a word I can construe.
404 line 1 lists கன்று among things that never grow horns, which clashes with the calf of 402; the word may be damaged.
409 line 4 ends with a doubled full stop (ஒத்தாய்..) and 413 line 4 has none.
396 line 4 joins the name as றேரனுமே, so the speaker's form is given as written.
